message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – processes many similar operations simultaneously. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) with powerful, complex control logic, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction. | Hundreds to thousands of simpler cores optimized for data‑parallel tasks. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, capable of executing a wide variety of instructions (arithmetic, logic, memory, I/O). | Optimized for SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – same instruction applied to many data elements at once. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches, deep pipelines, high clock speeds. | Smaller per‑core caches, but massive shared memory and fast on‑chip bandwidth. |
| **Typical workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, single‑thread performance (e.g., web browsing, office apps). | Highly parallel tasks: graphics rendering, scientific simulations, machine learning inference/training. |
| **Power & heat** | Higher power per core, but fewer cores overall. | Lower power per core, but many cores can still consume significant power; GPUs often have dedicated cooling. |
| **Programming model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded with complex scheduling. | Data‑parallel programming (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders). |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance and complex decision making, while GPUs shine when you can break a problem into many identical, independent operations that can run in parallel.
